text: So hi, thank you for coming to my talk.
So today I will be presenting an example of a hybrid
identification method using both deep learning
and interactive keys such as Expert3Keys
for insect identification. So a project that was
supported by the ECOPLUS project at Sorbonne
University.
So first, museum collections are a real treasure trove of data
that contain large amounts of data accumulated in the form
of specimens.
And this is really interesting because
there is a great precision in the taxonomy and the
identifications of those different specimens.
But this also allows us to capture a wide diversity of both
species and morphological variations that is present
in both collections.
And the collection data is increasingly made available in different
forms. So, for example, in
2D digitization,
which are photographs of specimens, but also
more recently in 3D scans that are made
available.
So the question that we are asking here is how can we effectively harness this
wealth of data, and what opportunities does it offer to improve
our understanding of biodiversity?
And so in this project, I was particularly interested in a
real pillar of biology, which is
taxonomic identification using
all of this data.
So we usually identify a taxon
from specimens by describing its different morphological
and color characteristics. And so traditionally, this has
been done by using
identification keys, where you describe the presence or absence
of a morphological character. And more recently, there has been
the development of interactive identification keys,
where the user can interactively
answer those presence or absence of characters.
Not one character at a time, but several characters at a time, reducing the
need for precise expertise and
the need for time for species
identification.
So even more recently, we have seen the development of automated identification
by using deep learning method, where you input some kind
of data from your specimen, and then it automatically
outputs a possible species identification.
So we have put two widely known ones.
So the first one is BirdNET for bird songs, and second one is a
PlantNET for plants images.
And so those methods are
less precise, usually in term of
taxonomic identification than the expert-based keys.
And they require a lot of training data
to work.
So here I was really interested in the opportunity to combine the precision
of identification keys with the automation power
of deep learning. And so my goal here was to develop hybrid
methods to get the best of both worlds.
So the idea is to input an image or photograph of
your specimen
in a deep learning model trained on the photographs of
collection specimens.
So the pros are, as I said, that you capture a wide range of
morphological variation, and you have precise identification,
meaning that you can control the quality of your database.
But those kind of ecological datasets are often small
compared to those typically used in deep learning and with a high
number of classes. So for example, high number of species.
And also there is a lot of imbalance in classes.
So
we often have a lot of data for one species and a few data for
another.
The goal will be to output the most probable taxon list that could
be then used to pre-filter the
interactive identification keys,
and to let the user have control over the final
decision on the species identification.
And so for this, I used
deep learning methods based on the supervised contrastive learning, and
more specifically, the SepCon method,
that are method that are specialized to learn similarity between
images.
So the way that this kind of method works
is based on pairs of positive images.
Positive meaning that they come from the same class, and so they are supposed to be
similar, such as the two number one on the left.
And pairs of negative images that come from different classes.
And so all of those images will go through a same
convolutional neural network, which are neural network that are specialized to
analyze image data.
And those network outputs a representation of the images in a reduced
dimensional space. So those are the representation vector
that are on the right of my slide.
And the way that the neural network learn is by
modifying its weight, so that representation vectors from
positive images are pulled together
in the representation space, and representation vector from
negative pairs are pushed apart.
And so in this way, we can learn the morphological discriminative features of
images that make them similar or dissimilar.
So I applied this method on a dataset of
French ladybirds, for which we already had an identification key
ready.
And I obtained images
of specimens from the Natural History Museum collection in
Paris for most of the same taxa.
The way I evaluated my model was by using a measure called the hit rate,
which means the success rate among the 10 nearest
neighbors. So meaning that for one image, you
get the 10 most probable taxon list, and if the right species
or the right taxon is in it, then the hit rate is one, and
if it's not, it's a zero.
And so we evaluate the performance using the average across all photograph.
So for example, if we have a hit rate of 80%, it means that the correct taxon is
found among the 10 nearest neighbor in 80% of the cases.
So after training, I obtained this embedding space where the
different phenotypic groups are clearly
separated and clustered together.
So I did a hyperparameter search by getting the model with
the highest hit rates on my validation data.
And so I won't get into the details, but
basically the selected model was a deep
network that could capture complex features that
had long training and moderate data augmentation.
So I gathered two different validation datasets to
evaluate the performance on external, previously unseen data.
So the first one I gathered from images from GBIF,
that is not standardized at all. So there is a lot of variation in both
lighting and pose. And the second one was much more
standardized. It's from a professional photography website.
And so I could see the performance on two kinds of
standardization levels.
And so I got a hit rate of about 90% for both of
the dataset, meaning that my model was able to generalize well
to external data.
So then we implemented
this model in Expertree by building this
little interface where the user can
input an image,
and then the
identification keys is automatically filtered based on the output of
the deep learning model. So here, for example, we have an example with a
Wikipedia illustration of the seven dot ladybirds, and as you can see, the
right species is in the filtered results.
But when we tested it, we saw that there was some kind of limitation when the
background was
too dark or too complex, and in general, when it's too different from our
training data set where the background was removed.
And so this is a limitation of the model.
And then I quantified again in a path length to the correct
identification, meaning that I counted the steps needed
in the ID key to get to the correct ID.
And so you can see that on the left you have without AI pre-filtering,
and on the right you have with AI pre-filtering.
And so we go from an average of 4.2 to one point steps
on average.
And interestingly, so the longer the path was without
AI filtering, the greater the reduction is after our AI
filtering. So the more complex cases of identifications are
greatly reduced by using AI pre-filtering,
meaning that we have less probability to make a
mistake during the
identification process.
So as a conclusion,
using the great wealth of data from museum
collections,
we combined the automation and flexibility of deep learning with
the explainability and precision of identification keys.
And this could lead to the reduce of the need for expertise
and the generalization to external data that could
be really useful, for example, in cases of the use of those ID keys
in a large-scale biodiversity monitoring, where the people
that are using those keys are rarely experts on the
specific taxa that are studied.
And as a perspective, we could now evaluate the increase in the
percentage of correct ID made by humans with and without AI,
because so I did a
theoretical quantification of
the gain
made by filtering with AI, but now we could test it with real humans.
Adding an automatic background removal step would
probably improve performance. And
lastly, I would be very interested in applying
this AI pre-filtering to other taxa for which we have an
identification key to see how well
this training workflow generalizes to other
taxa.
So yeah, thanks
you for your attention, and I'd like to thank again the ECOPLUS project
and my collaborators, so Sylvain Boucaud, Romain Latier, and Régine Vineuil-Neb
from Sorbonne University and the Muséum national d'Histoire naturelle.
